The United States Census Bureau publishes a table about surnames. For any surname held by at least a hundred Americans, it gives the share of the people carrying it who are white, Black, Asian, American Indian, Hispanic, or of two or more races. It is free, it requires no login, and between them its rows account for `r n(pop_covered)` people.

Multiply that table by a second public table, the racial make-up of the county somebody lives in, and out comes a probability that a named person belongs to a racial category. The procedure is called **Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding**. Elliott and colleagues (2009) developed it for health research, Imai and Khanna (2016) brought it into political science, and it is now routine evidence in federal voting-rights and lending-discrimination cases. Courts use it to decide how many Black voters a district contains.

Nothing in that description is a euphemism. Somebody's race is being inferred, without their knowledge, from their name and their address, by multiplying two spreadsheets published by their own government. So ask the plain question underneath. **Can a name tell you someone's race?**

## The test

Two federal tables answer it, because the method has exactly two ingredients and these are the published versions of both. The first is the Census Bureau's *Frequently Occurring Surnames* tabulation, in its 2010 edition (<https://www2.census.gov/topics/genealogy/2010surnames/names.zip>) and the 2020 edition that replaced it. The second is the Population Estimates Program's county file, vintage 2024: `r n(nrow(co))` counties in the same six categories.

There is no third public table that would do better, and what would genuinely be better is not a table at all. The honest input is a record of what people say about themselves. No such record exists in a voter file, and the reason is not cost: American states decided not to ask. The [BISG check brief](../bisg-check/bisg-check-brief.html) works in one of the few counties where a state did.

The two tables are joined through a person, which is where the assumptions stack up. [Join Keys and Crosswalks](../data-sources/data-sources-brief.html) is the reading on what a join key is and how one fails. It also covers the repair when two files carry different keys: a crosswalk, a table that translates one set of identifiers into another.

## The data

**Neither table was made for this.** The surname file sits under genealogy on the Bureau's servers, and its intended reader is somebody tracing a family. The county file is a different kind of number altogether: one is a count taken on a single day, the other a model carried forward a year at a time. The method multiplies them as though they were the same sort of object.

One row of the surname file looks like this.

```{r one-row}
```

The columns are `name`, `rank`, `count`, and the six shares `pctwhite`, `pctblack`, `pctapi`, `pctaian`, `pct2prace` and `pcthispanic`, which are mutually exclusive and sum to 100. The county file carries `fips`, `county`, `state`, `pop` and the same six groups.

The join runs on two keys and neither is a person. The **surname**, upper-cased, matches somebody to a row of the name table; the **five-digit county code** matches them to a row of the county table. Nothing joins the two tables to each other. A person is what makes them meet, and the assumption that both lists describe the same population at the same moment is a third assumption on top of each file's own.

Both tables needed cleaning, and one decision is the whole brief. In the 2010 file a cell too small to publish safely is written `(S)`. Read carelessly that is a zero; the build makes it a missing value instead, keeping the difference between *nobody* and *too few to say*. `r n(miss)` of the `r n(cells)` cells in the six percentage columns are withheld, `r pc(100 * miss / cells)`% of them, and dropping incomplete rows would throw away most American surnames.

The 2020 edition answers the same problem in the opposite way. It suppresses nothing, and instead publishes every count with noise added to protect the people in it. Noise added to a small count can push it below zero, so the Bureau ships the trimmed table and, beside it, the same table with the negatives left in. `r n(F20("rows_with_negative"))` of the `r n(F20("rows_2020"))` surnames carry at least one:

```{r neg2020}
```

Read the third and fourth columns together. The published file says no American Indian or Alaska Native person is named CHEUNG; the other, same office and same release, says minus two. **Minus two people is not a mistake. It is what the protection costs, made visible.** The method is most confident about a name in proportion to how lopsided that name is, so it is most sure of itself exactly where the file is least able to support it.

On the county side the build takes the July 2024 estimate for all ages, adds the male and female counts, and collapses the Bureau's categories down to the surname file's six.

***

> **Before you read on, write a ratio down.**
>
> Of the `r n(nrow(big))` surnames held by more than a thousand people, some
> number are more than 90% white and some number are more than 90% Black.
> **For every surname that is more than 90% Black, how many do you think are
> more than 90% white?** Four to one? Ten to one? Fifty to one?
>
> One ratio, on paper, before your eye reaches the figures below.

***

## What it says about democracy

Start with the thousand most common surnames, on the two shares that between them account for nearly all of their bearers.

```{r kilo-static, eval=!knitr::is_html_output(), fig.height=4.9}
```

```{r kilo-d3, results='asis', eval=knitr::is_html_output()}
```

**Figure 1. The thousand most common surnames in America, by the share of their bearers who are white and the share who are Black.** A scatter fits this question, because the question is whether the two shares trade off against each other. Each circle is one surname, sized by how many people hold it, and the diagonal is where a name with only white and Black bearers would have to sit. Together these names cover `r pc(k1_share)`% of everyone in the file. The right-hand wall is crowded and the top is empty: `r k1_w90` of the thousand are more than 90% white and `r k1_b90` are more than 90% Black, the highest point being `r k1_maxb$name` at `r pc(k1_maxb$pctblack)`%.

Three of those crowded middle points are the commonest names in America:

```{r ambiguous}
```

**Williams is `r pc(G("WILLIAMS","pctwhite"))`% white and `r pc(G("WILLIAMS","pctblack"))`% Black**, and it is the `r G("WILLIAMS","rank")`rd most common surname in America, held by `r n(G("WILLIAMS","count"))` people. Smith and Johnson are ranks `r G("SMITH","rank")` and `r G("JOHNSON","rank")`. For names like these the surname settles nothing, and that is not rare: for `r pc(p_useless)`% of the people this file covers, no group reaches 60%.

Now count past the 90% line, on every surname held by more than a thousand people.

```{r asym-prep, include=FALSE}
```

```{r asym-static, eval=!knitr::is_html_output(), fig.height=4.6}
```

```{r asym-d3, results='asis', eval=knitr::is_html_output()}
```

**Figure 2. How many surnames are more than 90% one group.** The axis is logarithmic, so equal distances are equal *multiples* rather than equal counts, which is why these are dots to be read by position and not bars to be read by length.

`r n(n90[["white"]])` surnames are more than 90% white. `r n(n90[["Black"]])` are more than 90% Black. That is a ratio of about `r alab`, for a group that is roughly `r pc(100*natl[["black"]], 0)`% of the country rather than one-hundredth of it. Compare it with the ratio you wrote down. Four or five to one is the reasonable expectation, and it is wrong by more than an order of magnitude. **The group the Voting Rights Act was written to protect is the group whose surnames carry the least information.**

That is not a quirk of the data and not a flaw in the Bureau's processing. It is history sitting in a spreadsheet. Enslaved people were given, or took, the surnames of enslavers, and after emancipation those names stayed. Black and white Americans have shared a common stock of surnames for a hundred and sixty years. The exceptions show the mechanism from the other side. Washington is the most identifiably Black common surname in America, `r pc(G("WASHINGTON","pctblack"))`% of the `r n(G("WASHINGTON","count"))` people who carry it, because freed people took the names of presidents associated with liberty.

So what carries the inference for everybody else? The address. Bayes' rule combines the two tables in one line: the probability that a person of surname $s$ in county $g$ belongs to group $r$ is

$$P(r \mid s, g) \;\propto\; \frac{P(r \mid s)\,P(r \mid g)}{P(r)}$$

Dividing by the national share $P(r)$ stops the arithmetic double-counting the fact that some groups are large everywhere. That national share is the base rate, and it does more work than anything else here. Watch what it does to the commonest name in the country:

```{r flip}
```

**Smith is `r pc(G("SMITH","pctwhite"))`% white nationally. A Smith in the Bronx is `r pc(bisg("SMITH","36005")[["black"]])`% Black.** The name did not change; the arithmetic stopped ignoring where the person lives. Lee runs the other way, resolving to `r pc(bisg("LEE","42003")[["white"]])`% white in Allegheny County and `r pc(bisg("LEE","15003")[["api"]])`% Asian in Honolulu. Three letters, opposite conclusions.

```{r gains-static, eval=!knitr::is_html_output(), fig.height=3.8}
```

```{r gains-d3, results='asis', eval=knitr::is_html_output()}
```

**Figure 3. How much six surnames move when one county is added.** Each rod is one surname: the hollow end is the strongest claim the name alone will support, the solid end is the strongest claim it supports once the person is placed in the Bronx.

`r rownames(gd)[1]` barely moves. `r rownames(gd)[nrow(gd)]` moves `r sprintf("%+.1f", gd[nrow(gd), "change"])` points. That is Bayes' rule behaving correctly, because a sharp starting guess is hard to move and a flat one is easy. But follow the consequence. The names that need help are the *common* ones: Smith, Johnson and Williams are three of the five most frequent surnames in America. Nguyen and Garcia are precise, and describe a much smaller share of it.

**So for most Americans this is substantially a method for inferring race from an address.** Told only the name, you would learn almost nothing; told only the county, you would learn most of what the model produces. The consequence is worth saying rather than implying. **The method is accurate because American neighbourhoods are segregated.** It works well in the Bronx precisely to the extent that the Bronx is not integrated, so the estimate borrows its precision from the condition the Voting Rights Act exists to address.

## What this brief cannot tell you

**Nothing here has been checked against a known answer.** Every number above describes what the method *does*, not how often it is right, and those are different questions. The [BISG check brief](../bisg-check/bisg-check-brief.html) is the test; this one is the anatomy.

**Nor can any of it be said about an individual.** The output is a statement about a population: of all the Smiths in the Bronx, roughly `r pc(bisg("SMITH","36005")[["black"]])`% are Black. Every use of the method takes a number true on average and attaches it to somebody in particular.

**The two tables describe different years.** The surname list is a count from a census; the county file is a model carried forward to 2024. Anyone born or arrived in between sits in one file and not the other, and no column in either says how much that costs.

**And a name absent from the file cannot be scored at all.** The Bureau publishes no surname held by fewer than `r n(min(sn$count))` people, so Americans with the rarest names are not classified badly by this method. They are outside it. County is also coarse: the standard software works down to the census block, where the inference leans even harder on segregation.

## What you should have learned

- The whole method is one line of arithmetic: what a name implies, times what a county implies, divided by the national share of each group.
- The name carries almost nothing for most Americans. `r k1_b90` of the thousand commonest surnames are more than 90% Black, and for `r pc(p_useless)`% of the people this file covers no group reaches 60%.
- Of the `r n(nrow(big))` surnames held by more than a thousand people, `r n(n90[["white"]])` are more than 90% white and `r n(n90[["Black"]])` more than 90% Black, a ratio of about `r alab` for a group that is `r pc(100*natl[["black"]], 0)`% of the country.
- Geography supplies what the name cannot. Smith is `r pc(G("SMITH","pctwhite"))`% white nationally and `r pc(bisg("SMITH","36005")[["black"]])`% Black in the Bronx, and the name that gains most from one county gains `r sprintf("%+.1f", gd[nrow(gd), "change"])` points.
- Neither edition of the file can give you a small cell you can trust: 2010 withholds `r n(miss)` cells outright, and 2020 publishes noised counts that go negative in `r n(F20("rows_with_negative"))` of `r n(F20("rows_2020"))` surnames.

## Extensions

None of these is answered above, and every one can be answered by sorting or grouping the tables the Sources section hands over.

- `census_surnames.csv` and `census_surnames_2010.csv` hold the same names fourteen years apart. Join them on `name` and find the surnames whose `pctblack` moved most. Is that people changing, or the table changing?
- `surnames_2020_negatives.csv` shows cells published as zero that are negative in the research copy. Pick a row and explain what a negative count of people is.
- `county_race.csv` gives each county's racial shares. Take a surname from `census_surnames.csv`, apply the arithmetic above to one county, then find a county where the answer is very different.
- `census_surnames.csv` covers only names held by enough people to publish. Sort by `count` and work out roughly how many Americans have a name too rare to appear.

Two stretch ideas point past the spreadsheet. The `wru` package implements the real version, with first names, age, sex and geography down to the census block. Run it on one name, and see how much of the extra sharpness comes from the finer geography. And the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau published its own version of this method in 2014 for lending cases; read what it says about error rates against what the tables above imply.

## Sources

**Data**

- U.S. Census Bureau, *Frequently Occurring Surnames from the 2010 Census* —
  every surname held by 100 or more people, with the racial composition of its
  bearers, and cells too small to publish safely suppressed.
  <https://www2.census.gov/topics/genealogy/2010surnames/names.zip>
- U.S. Census Bureau, *Frequently Occurring Surnames from the 2020 Census*,
  published twice: once trimmed, once with the negatives left in.
  <https://www.census.gov/topics/population/genealogy/data/2020_surnames.html>
- U.S. Census Bureau, Population Estimates Program, county characteristics
  file for 2024, collapsed to the same six categories.
  <https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2024/counties/asrh/>

**Literature**

- Elliott, M. N., Morrison, P. A., Fremont, A., McCaffrey, D. F., Pantoja, P.
  and Lurie, N. (2009). "Using the Census Bureau's Surname List to Improve
  Estimates of Race/Ethnicity and Associated Disparities." *Health Services and
  Outcomes Research Methodology* 9(2): 69–83.
- Imai, K. and Khanna, K. (2016). "Improving Ecological Inference by Predicting
  Individual Ethnicity from Voter Registration Records." *Political Analysis*
  24(2): 263–272.
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (2014). *Using Publicly Available
  Information to Proxy for Unidentified Race and Ethnicity.*
- *Thornburg v. Gingles*, 478 U.S. 30 (1986).
